title: The hill that drained a reservoir
teaches: Where Seattle's water comes from, and the Masonry Dam's leak through glacial gravel in 1918
summary: **Seattle drinks from two Cascade rivers.** The Cedar gives about two thirds of the water for about 1.5 million people, the South Fork Tolt the other third.
**The Cedar's water is not filtered.** Its watershed is owned by the city and closed to the public, so the water is only treated with ozone and ultraviolet light to kill germs.
**The city takes about an eighth of the Cedar's water.** About 0.11 km³ a year goes to taps out of roughly 0.9 km³ of rain and snow on the watershed; the rest goes back to the air or down the river.
**The Masonry Dam stands beside a moraine.** The ridge on one side of its reservoir is sand and gravel the ice sheet left, not rock.
**Water seeps through gravel by Darcy's law.** The flow is the conductivity of the ground, times the push (how steeply the water table falls), times the area the water flows through.
**A deeper reservoir leaks much more.** Doubling the water's depth against a gravel bank doubles both the push and the soaked thickness of gravel, so the seepage roughly quadruples.

**Seepage that carries grains is dangerous.** Springs that wash sand out of a slope hollow it from below, and in December 1918 the hillside above Boxley Creek burst and the flood destroyed the town of Edgewick.
**The reservoir is still kept low.** The city never filled the Masonry Pool to the height it was built for, and water from the Cedar still seeps through the moraine toward the Snoqualmie.

parts.title: A flood from the wrong valley

blocks.text: Just before Christmas in 1918, a flood of water, mud, boulders and logs came down Boxley Creek, a small stream in the Cascade foothills east of North Bend, and swept through the mill town of Edgewick where the creek meets the South Fork of the Snoqualmie River. It wrecked the mill and the houses near the creek and tore out the Milwaukee Road's railway line where it crossed the creek on the hillside above.[^date] Edgewick was never rebuilt.

Boxley Creek is a small stream draining a small patch of hillside, and no rain on that hillside could have made a flood like this. The water had come from just over a low ridge to the south, from the reservoir Seattle had built in the Cedar River's valley, behind a concrete wall called the Masonry Dam. The dam itself held. It never cracked or spilled over. The water went another way, through the hill beside it.

Before reading on, look at the map below and see if you can work out how water held behind a solid dam in one valley could come out in another valley, more than a kilometre away and well downhill. Lesson 3, on groundwater and Darcy's law, holds the answer.

blocks.caption: Seattle's two sources, on a shaded map of the ground's height with north at the top. Find the Masonry Dam, then Rattlesnake Lake and Edgewick just north of it, on the far side of a low ridge: that side drains north to the Snoqualmie. The lakes in the hills are not coloured as water here.

blocks.text: Every tap in Seattle, and in many of the towns around it, draws on two rivers in the Cascades. The Cedar River supplies about two thirds of the water for about 1.5 million people; the South Fork of the Tolt River, to the north, supplies the rest. On the Cedar, the city owns almost the whole upper watershed, some 370 square kilometres of forest (about 90,000 acres), and keeps it closed. No one lives in it and no one may walk in it without a permit. Rain and snow that land there run through forest soil and into the river with nothing upstream to dirty them.

The water is stored in Chester Morse Lake and in the smaller pool behind the Masonry Dam, then let down the river to Landsburg, some 20 km downstream, where most of what the city takes is drawn off into pipelines. They carry it to Lake Youngs, a storage reservoir south-east of the city, where a treatment plant kills germs in the water with ozone and ultraviolet light before it goes on to the city. The Cedar's water is not filtered. A source this clean, from a watershed this well guarded, is allowed to skip that step, and Seattle is one of only a handful of large American cities that does.[^unfiltered] The Tolt's water is filtered.

**An estimate.** The Cedar watershed gets something like 2.5 metres of rain and snow a year on average, much more on the crest than near Landsburg. Spread over 370 km², which is 370 million square metres, that is about 900 million cubic metres, or 0.9 km³, a year. The whole supply system, both rivers, delivers something like 0.17 km³ a year. The Cedar's two thirds of that is about 0.11 km³, and 0.11 out of 0.9 is about an eighth. So the city takes roughly an eighth of what falls on the Cedar's watershed. Of the other seven eighths, part goes back to the air from leaves and the ground, as lesson 1 described, and the rest runs on down the Cedar to Lake Washington. Under an agreement the city signed with federal and state agencies in 2000, it must leave set flows in the river for its salmon.

blocks.caption: Water in a year on the Cedar, in cubic kilometres: the rain and snow on the closed watershed (pale blue, falling water), what the region's taps draw from both rivers (purple, people's works) and the Cedar's share of that (blue, river water). The Cedar's share is about an eighth of the rain and snow. Rough figures.

parts.title: A dam beside a heap of gravel

blocks.text: The Masonry Dam was finished in 1914, in a narrow rocky part of the Cedar's valley a little upstream of Cedar Falls, the small settlement by the city's power station. The reservoir behind it is called the Masonry Pool. The dam's foundations are in rock. The trouble was beside it. On the north side, the pool rests against a broad, low ridge that is not rock at all but a **moraine**: a heap of sand, gravel and boulders dropped by the edge of the ice sheet that filled the Puget lowland until some 16,000 years ago (the Geology course on this site tells that story).[^moraine] The ice pushed a tongue up the Cedar's valley and left this heap as a dam across it. The moraine now forms the low divide between the Cedar and the South Fork of the Snoqualmie. On its far side the ground drops away, well below the reservoir, to Rattlesnake Lake and the head of Boxley Creek.

Lesson 3 showed what water does in ground like this. It moves through the spaces between the grains, and **Darcy's law** sets how fast: the flow is the ground's conductivity (how easily it passes water), times the push (how steeply the [[water table|ground]] falls along the way), times the area the water flows through. Conductivity covers an enormous range. Clean gravel passes water something like a million times faster than clay, and a moraine is often full of clean gravel. Put a reservoir against one side of a gravel ridge, with lower ground on the other side, and water will flow through the ridge and come out as [[springs|water]] wherever the far slope cuts the water table.

blocks.caption: A model of the moraine, in section: the reservoir on the left, the gravel bank, and springs where the water comes out at the foot of the far side. One slider sets how high the reservoir stands against the bank, the other what the bank is made of. The flow is figured for a bank 1.5 km thick from reservoir to springs and 3 km long along the shore; the real moraine's size and makeup are only roughly known.
blocks.task: Guess how much more seeps through, then raise the reservoir from 20 m to 40 m

blocks.text: The answer surprises most people. Picture the bank in the figure, with the reservoir against one face and the springs at the foot of the other. The push is how far the water table drops between the two, over the width of the bank; with the springs at the bottom, that drop is just the depth of the reservoir, so twice the depth means twice the push. The water flows through the soaked gravel below the water table, and on the reservoir side that soaked layer is as thick as the water is deep, so twice the depth also means twice the area to flow through. Darcy's law multiplies the two: twice times twice is four times as much seepage.[^dupuit] A test of the reservoir at a low level could look reassuring and still say little about the reservoir full. The other slider changes the ground: each step toward coarser gravel multiplies the seepage by ten or more.

The first warning came in 1915. As the new reservoir rose, Rattlesnake Lake, on the far side of the moraine, began to rise too, though nothing new was flowing into it on the surface. It rose until it flooded the small railway town of Moncton on its shore, and the city ended up taking over the town's land.[^moncton] The reservoir was leaking: water was seeping out of it through the hill, and a great deal of it.

Seattle's engineers went on raising the reservoir, and in late 1918 it stood higher than it ever had. The springs at the head of Boxley Creek, on the far side of the moraine, grew. Water coming out of a slope fast enough can carry the grains around it along with it. The carving starts at the foot of the far slope, where the water comes out, and a hollow grows backward into the hill toward the reservoir. The longer the hollow, the less unbroken gravel is left between it and the reservoir, so the same drop in level acts over a shorter distance, the push grows, more water comes through, and it carries more grains. Engineers call this runaway **piping**, and it is how many earth dams and levees fail.[^piping]

In December 1918 the side of the moraine at the head of Boxley Creek gave way. Water stored in the gravel, and water from the reservoir behind it, poured out down the creek, carving a canyon as it went, and the flood reached Edgewick. Histories of the burst record a town lost but no lives lost. The city faced years of claims for the damage.

blocks.title: A common mistake
points: People often picture a dam failing when its wall breaks. Plenty of dams and levees fail around or under their walls instead: water finds a way through the ground beside or beneath them, and once it carries grains, the way grows. The Masonry Dam never broke.

blocks.text: After 1918 the city never filled the Masonry Pool to the height the dam was built for. It is kept lower, the dam serves mainly to steady the river and feed the Cedar Falls power station below it, and most of the Cedar's storage is in Chester Morse Lake upstream. Water still seeps through the moraine: Rattlesnake Lake rises and falls through the year with the water behind it, fed from underground across the divide.

**Go and look.** Rattlesnake Lake, a short drive past North Bend beside the Cedar River Watershed Education Center, is open to everyone. Walk its shore and look for a surface stream big enough to fill it; there is none that could. In a dry autumn, when the lake is low, stumps of the forest that stood there before 1915 stand out of the water and the mud. The climb to Rattlesnake Ledge looks down over the lake and across the low, wooded moraine toward the Cedar valley on the other side.

blocks.caption: Six questions on the Cedar and the moraine
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Where does most of Seattle's tap water come from?
choices: The Cedar River, with the rest from the Tolt River
Lake Washington, drawn from intakes off Mercer Island
Deep wells in the gravels under south King County
The Snoqualmie River, piped west from below the falls
items.why: Two Cascade rivers supply the city: the Cedar about two thirds and the South Fork Tolt about a third.

items.ask: Seattle treats the Cedar's water with ozone and ultraviolet light but does not filter it. What makes that allowed?
choices: The city keeps the watershed closed, so little dirties the water
Snowmelt is cleaner than rain, and the Cedar is mostly snowmelt
The water settles clean in Lake Washington before it is drawn off
Ultraviolet light removes particles as well as killing germs
items.why: A closed, protected watershed keeps the water clean enough that killing germs is enough. Filtering removes particles, which ozone and ultraviolet light do not.

items.ask: The Cedar watershed gets about 0.9 km³ of rain and snow a year, and the city draws about 0.11 km³ a year from the Cedar. Where does most of the rest go?
choices: Back to the air, or on down the river to Lake Washington
Into the Masonry Pool, which stores it from year to year
Through the moraine into the Snoqualmie, as seepage
Deep into the rock, where it refills an aquifer under Seattle
items.why: Some returns to the air from leaves and soil, and most of the rest runs down the Cedar; the reservoirs store only a season's water.

items.ask: Why could water held behind the Masonry Dam reach Boxley Creek in the next valley?
choices: The ridge between them is glacial gravel that passes water
A crack in the dam's concrete let water out under the river
Water evaporated from the reservoir and fell again as rain
A flood spilled over the top of the ridge in a wet winter
items.why: The ridge is a moraine of sand and gravel, and the reservoir stood above the ground beyond it, so water flowed through it by Darcy's law.

items.ask: Water stands 20 m deep against a gravel bank, with springs at the foot of the far side. It rises to 40 m. Roughly how much more seeps through?
choices: About four times as much
About twice as much
About the same
A little less
items.why: The push and the soaked thickness of gravel both double, and Darcy's law multiplies them.

items.ask: Springs at the foot of a slope start to carry out sand. Why is that a warning?
choices: The hollow they cut grows back toward the water, and the flow speeds up
Sandy water weighs more and pushes the whole slope over at once
The sand will settle in the reservoir and raise it until it overflows
Sand blocks the springs, and the trapped water bursts out elsewhere
items.why: As the hollow eats back, the gravel left between it and the water gets thinner, so the push grows and more grains go: piping.

date.title: The Boxley burst
date.text: The flood is usually dated to 23 December 1918 and called the Boxley burst, after the creek. The railway was the Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul's line over Snoqualmie Pass (the Milwaukee Road), which ran past Rattlesnake Lake and crossed Boxley Creek on the slope above the town.

unfiltered.title: Skipping the filter
unfiltered.text: Federal drinking-water rules require water from rivers and lakes to be filtered unless the source is very clean and the utility controls what happens in its watershed. Filtering takes out particles; ozone and ultraviolet light kill bacteria and the small parasites that chlorine alone can miss. Seattle added the ozone and ultraviolet treatment for the Cedar in the early 2000s.

moraine.title: Moraine
moraine.text: A moraine is the debris a glacier or ice sheet leaves where its edge stood: everything from clay to boulders, often washed by meltwater into beds of clean sand and gravel. Clean gravel is among the most permeable kinds of ground there are.

dupuit.title: Dupuit's rule
dupuit.text: The French engineer Jules Dupuit worked out in 1863 how water flows through a level bed of gravel with the water table as its top. With springs at the foot of the far side, the flow goes as the square of the water's depth at the high side. The figure uses his rule.

moncton.title: Moncton
moncton.text: Moncton was a stop on the Milwaukee Road at Rattlesnake Lake. When the lake flooded it in 1915 its people sued the city, and the city took over the land. Little of the town remains.

piping.title: Piping
piping.text: Piping starts where seepage leaves the ground, at the toe of a slope (its foot) or of a levee, where the water's push can lift grains free. Engineers watch for sand boils, muddy springs bubbling up behind a levee in flood, for this reason, and lay filters of sand and gravel sorted by size at the toes of earth dams, so that water can leave but grains cannot.
